the latter broke from it again, forcefully asserting the supremacy of <color=#3366CC>Anglicanism</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Elizabethan era</color> is the epoch in
the Tudor age of the reign of Queen Elizabeth I ("the Virgin Queen"). Historians often depict it as the golden age in
English history that represented the apogee of the English Renaissance and saw the flowering of great art, drama,
poetry, music and literature. England during this period had a centralised, well-organised, and effective government.
Competing with <color=#3366CC>Spain</color>, the first English colony in the Americas was founded in 1585 by explorer <color=#3366CC>Walter Raleigh</color> in
<color=#3366CC>Virginia</color> and named <color=#3366CC>Roanoke</color>. The Roanoke colony failed and is known as the lost colony after it was found abandoned
on the return of the late-arriving supply ship. With the <color=#3366CC>East India Company</color>, England also competed with the <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color> and
<color=#3366CC>French</color> in the East. During the Elizabethan period, England was at war with Spain. An <color=#3366CC>armada</color> sailed from Spain in
1588 as part of a wider plan to invade England and re-establish a Catholic monarchy. This plan was thwarted by bad
coordination, stormy weather and successful harrying attacks by an English fleet under <color=#3366CC>Lord Howard of Effingham</color>. The
failure of the 1588 expedition did not deter Spain, which launched two further armadas in 1596 and 1597; however,
these subsequent fleets were likewise dispersed by severe Atlantic storms.
Union with Scotland and English Civil War
The political structure of the island changed in 1603, when <color=#3366CC>James VI</color>, King of Scots, inherited the English throne as
James I, thereby creating a personal union between the two rival realms. He styled himself King of Great Britain,
although this had no basis in English law. Under the auspices of James VI and I the Authorised <color=#3366CC>King James Version</color> of
the Holy Bible was published in 1611. It was the standard version of the Bible read by most Protestant Christians for
four hundred years until modern revisions were produced in the 20th century.
Based on conflicting political, religious and social positions, the <color=#3366CC>English Civil War</color> was fought between the supporters of
Parliament and those of King <color=#3366CC>Charles I</color>, known colloquially as Roundheads and Cavaliers respectively. This was an
interwoven part of the wider multifaceted <color=#3366CC>Wars of the Three Kingdoms</color>, involving <color=#3366CC>Scotland</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ireland</color>. The
Parliamentarians were victorious, <color=#3366CC>Charles I was executed</color> and the kingdom replaced by the Commonwealth. Leader of
the Parliament forces, <color=#3366CC>Oliver Cromwell</color> declared himself Lord Protector in 1653; a period of <color=#3366CC>personal rule</color> followed. After
Cromwell's death and the resignation of his son Richard as Lord Protector, <color=#3366CC>Charles II</color> was invited to return as monarch
in 1660, in a move called the <color=#3366CC>Restoration</color>. With the reopening of theatres, fine arts, literature and performing arts
flourished throughout the Restoration of the "Merry Monarch" Charles II. After the <color=#3366CC>Glorious Revolution</color> of 1688, it was
constitutionally established that King and Parliament should rule together, though <color=#3366CC>Parliament</color> would have the real
power. This was established with the <color=#3366CC>Bill of Rights</color> in 1689. Amongst the statutes set down were that the law could only
be made by Parliament and could not be suspended by the King, also that the King could not impose taxes or raise an
army without the prior approval of Parliament. Also since that time, no British monarch has entered the <color=#3366CC>House of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Commons</color> when it is sitting, which is annually commemorated at the State Opening of Parliament by the British
monarch when the doors of the House of Commons are slammed in the face of the monarch's messenger, symbolising
the rights of Parliament and its independence from the monarch. With the founding of the <color=#3366CC>Royal Society</color> in 1660,
science was greatly encouraged.
In 1666 the <color=#3366CC>Great Fire of London</color> gutted the city of London, but it was rebuilt shortly afterward with many significant
buildings designed by Sir <color=#3366CC>Christopher Wren</color>. By the mid-to-late 17th century, two political factions had emerged – the
Tories and Whigs. Though the Tories initially supported Catholic king <color=#3366CC>James II</color>, some of them, along with the Whigs,
during the <color=#3366CC>Revolution of 1688</color> invited the Dutch <color=#3366CC>Prince William of Orange</color> to defeat James and become the king. Some
English people, primarily in the north, were <color=#3366CC>Jacobites</color> and continued to support James and his sons. Under the Stuart
dynasty England expanded in trade, finance and prosperity. The Royal Navy developed Europe's largest merchant
fleet. After the parliaments of England and Scotland agreed, the two countries joined in political union, to create the
<color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Great Britain</color> in 1707. To accommodate the union, institutions such as the law and national churches of
each remained separate.
Late modern and contemporary periods
Following the formation of the Kingdom of Great Britain, output from the Royal Society and other <color=#3366CC>English initiatives</color>
combined with the <color=#3366CC>Scottish Enlightenment</color> to create innovations in science and engineering, while the enormous growth
in British overseas trade protected by the <color=#3366CC>Royal Navy</color> paved the way for the establishment of the <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color>.
Domestically it drove the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>, a period of profound change in the socioeconomic and cultural
conditions of England, resulting in industrialised agriculture, manufacture, engineering and mining, as well as new and
pioneering road, rail and water networks to facilitate their expansion and development. The opening of Northwest
England's <color=#3366CC>Bridgewater Canal</color> in 1761 ushered in the canal age in Britain. In 1825 the world's first permanent steam
locomotive-hauled passenger railway – the Stockton and Darlington Railway – opened to the public.
During the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>, many workers moved from England's countryside to new and expanding urban
industrial areas to work in factories, for instance at <color=#3366CC>Birmingham</color> and <color=#3366CC>Manchester</color>, with the latter the world's first
industrial city. England maintained relative stability throughout the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color>, under <color=#3366CC>George III</color> and <color=#3366CC>William Pitt</color>
<color=#3366CC>the Younger</color>. The regency of George IV is noted for its elegance and achievements in the fine arts and architecture.
During the <color=#3366CC>Napoleonic Wars</color>, <color=#3366CC>Napoleon</color> planned to invade from the south-east; however, this failed to manifest and the
Napoleonic forces were defeated by the British: at sea by <color=#3366CC>Horatio Nelson</color>, and on land by <color=#3366CC>Arthur Wellesley</color>. The victory
at the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Trafalgar</color> confirmed the naval supremacy Britain had established during the eighteenth century. The
Napoleonic Wars fostered a concept of Britishness and a united national British people, shared with the English, Scots
and Welsh.
London became the largest and most populous metropolitan area in the world during the <color=#3366CC>Victorian era</color>, and trade within
the British Empire – as well as the standing of the British military and navy – was prestigious. Technologically, this era
saw many innovations that proved key to the United Kingdom's power and prosperity. Political agitation at home from
radicals such as the <color=#3366CC>Chartists</color> and the <color=#3366CC>suffragettes</color> enabled legislative reform and <color=#3366CC>universal suffrage</color>.
Power shifts in east-central Europe led to World War I; hundreds of thousands of English soldiers died fighting for the
United Kingdom as part of the <color=#3366CC>Allies</color>. Two decades later, in <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, the United Kingdom was again one of the
<color=#3366CC>Allies</color>. Developments in warfare technology saw many cities damaged by air-raids during <color=#3366CC>the Blitz</color>. Following the war,
the British Empire experienced rapid <color=#3366CC>decolonisation</color>, and there was a speeding-up of technological innovations;
automobiles became the primary means of transport and Frank Whittle's development of the <color=#3366CC>jet engine</color> led to wider air
travel. Residential patterns were altered in England by private motoring, and by the creation of the National Health
Service in 1948, providing publicly funded health care to all permanent residents free at the point of need. Combined,
these prompted the reform of local government in England in the mid-20th century.
Since the 20th century, there has been significant population movement to England, mostly from other parts of the
<color=#3366CC>British Isles</color>, but also from the <color=#3366CC>Commonwealth</color>, particularly the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>. Since the 1970s there has been a
large move away from manufacturing and an increasing emphasis on the service industry. As part of the <color=#3366CC>United</color>
<color=#3366CC>Kingdom</color>, the area joined a common market initiative called the <color=#3366CC>European Economic Community</color> which became the
<color=#3366CC>European Union</color>.
Since the late 20th century the <color=#3366CC>administration of the United Kingdom</color> has moved towards devolved governance in
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. England and Wales continues to exist as a jurisdiction within the United
Kingdom. Devolution has stimulated a greater emphasis on a more English-specific identity and patriotism. There is no
devolved English government, but an attempt to create a similar system on a sub-regional basis was rejected by
referendum.
Governance
England is part of the United Kingdom, a <color=#3366CC>constitutional monarchy</color> with a <color=#3366CC>parliamentary system</color>. There has not been a
government of England since 1707, when the <color=#3366CC>Acts of Union 1707</color>, putting into effect the terms of the Treaty of Union,
joined England and Scotland to form the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Great Britain</color>. Before the union England was ruled by its monarch
and the Parliament of England.
England is governed directly by the <color=#3366CC>Parliament of the United Kingdom</color>, although other countries of the United Kingdom
have devolved governments. There has been debate about how to counterbalance this in England. Originally it was
planned that various regions of England would be devolved, but following the proposal's rejection by the North East in a
2004 referendum, this has not been carried out. In 2024, an England-only intergovernmental body, known as the
Mayoral Council for England, was established to bring together ministers from the <color=#3366CC>UK Government</color>, the Mayor of
London and the leaders of combined authorities.
In 2026 the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 received royal assent and established a three
tier system of Governance consisting of National, Strategic Authorities and Principal Authorities.
Politics
In the <color=#3366CC>House of Commons</color> which is the lower house of the British Parliament based at the <color=#3366CC>Palace of Westminster</color>, there
are 543 members of parliament (MPs) for constituencies in England, out of the 650 total. England is represented by
347 MPs from the <color=#3366CC>Labour Party</color>, 116 from the <color=#3366CC>Conservative Party</color>, 65 from the Liberal Democrats, four for Reform UK
and four for the Green Party of England and Wales.
Tiers of Governance
There are currently three overarching categories of governance in England, these include National, Strategic Authority
and Principal Authorities.
National
England does not have its own Devolved Parliament similar to the Scottish Parliament, Welsh Senedd and Northern
Ireland Assembly and requires the <color=#3366CC>U.K Parliament</color> to create legislation for England.
Strategic Authority
Strategic Authority is a sub-regional category consisting of Combined Authorities/County Combined Authorities and the
Greater London Authority.
As of 2026 there are currently 18 Combined/ County Combined Authorities in England with 16 of those having a directly
elected mayor.
From 1994 until the early 2010s England was divided for a few purposes into regions; a 1998 referendum for the
London Region created the London Assembly two years later. A failed 2004 North East England devolution referendum
cancelled further regional assembly devolution with the regional structure outside London abolished.
Principal authorities
Principal Authorities consist of unitary councils, district councils and county councils. Outside the London region,
England's highest tier is the 48 ceremonial counties. These are used primarily as a geographical frame of reference. Of
these, 38 have developed gradually since the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>; these were reformed to 51 in 1974 and to their current
number in 1996. Each has a Lord Lieutenant and a High Sheriff; these appointees represent the British monarch
locally. Some counties, such as <color=#3366CC>Herefordshire</color>, are only divided further into civil parishes. The royal county of <color=#3366CC>Berkshire</color>
and the metropolitan counties have a different status from other ceremonial counties. In 1974, the Local Government
Act 1972 created a two-tier system in England with 39 non-metropolitan (shire) counties and 6 metropolitan counties.
The shire counties were two-tier (county council + district councils), while the metropolitan counties had a different
division of functions.
The metropolitan county councils were abolished in 1986. Further reforms in the mid-1990s (mainly 1995–1998)
replaced two-tier structures with unitary authorities in many areas. The 1996 changes formally separated ceremonial
counties (for lieutenancy and ceremonial purposes) from administrative counties (for local government).
This created clearer distinction: ceremonial counties often follow historic or adjusted boundaries, while administrative
areas reflect current unitary or two-tier council structures.
Administratively, London comprises 32 London boroughs and the <color=#3366CC>City of London</color>. The 32 London boroughs form the
ceremonial county of Greater London, with the City of London being a separate ceremonial county.
England is also divided into local government districts. The district can align to a ceremonial county, or be a district tier
within a shire county, be a royal or metropolitan borough, have borough or city status, or be a unitary authority, London
for example has 33 local government districts.
At the community level, much of England is divided into civil parishes with their own councils; in Greater London only
one such parish, Queen's Park, exists as of 2014 after they were abolished in 1965 until legislation allowed their
recreation in 2007.
Law
The English law legal system, developed over the centuries, is the basis of <color=#3366CC>common law</color> legal systems used in most
<color=#3366CC>Commonwealth</color> countries and the United States (except <color=#3366CC>Louisiana</color>). Despite now being part of the United Kingdom, the
legal system of the <color=#3366CC>Courts of England and Wales</color> continued, under the Treaty of Union, as a separate legal system
from the one used in Scotland. The general essence of English law is that it is made by judges sitting in courts,
applying their common sense and knowledge of <color=#3366CC>legal precedent</color> – stare decisis – to the facts before them.
The court system is headed by the Senior Courts of England and Wales, consisting of the Court of Appeal, the High
Court of Justice for civil cases, and the Crown Court for criminal cases. The <color=#3366CC>Supreme Court of the United Kingdom</color> is
the highest court for criminal and civil cases in England and Wales. It was created in 2009 after constitutional changes,
taking over the judicial functions of the House of Lords. A decision of the Supreme Court is binding on every other court
in the hierarchy, which must follow its directions.
The secretary of state for justice is the minister responsible to Parliament for the judiciary, the court system and prisons
and probation in England. Crime increased between 1981 and 1995 but fell by 42% in the period 1995–2006. The
prison population doubled over the same period, giving it one of the highest incarceration rates in Western Europe at
147 per 100,000. His Majesty's Prison Service, reporting to the Ministry of Justice, manages most prisons, housing in
2024 around 87,300 prisoners in England and Wales, the most since 1900.
Geography
Landscape and rivers
Geographically, England includes the central and southern two-thirds of the island of Great Britain, plus such offshore
islands as the <color=#3366CC>Isle of Wight</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Isles of Scilly</color>. It is bordered by two other countries of the United Kingdom: to the
north by Scotland and to the west by <color=#3366CC>Wales</color>.
England is closer than any other part of mainland Britain to the European continent. It is separated from <color=#3366CC>France</color>
(Hauts-de-France) by a 21 mi sea gap, though the two countries are connected by the <color=#3366CC>Channel Tunnel</color> near
Folkestone. England also has shores on the <color=#3366CC>Irish Sea</color>, <color=#3366CC>North Sea</color> and Atlantic Ocean.

The ports of London, <color=#3366CC>Liverpool</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Newcastle</color> lie on the tidal rivers <color=#3366CC>Thames</color>, Mersey and <color=#3366CC>Tyne</color>, respectively. At 220
mi, the <color=#3366CC>Severn</color> is the longest river flowing through England. It empties into the Bristol Channel and is notable for its
Severn Bore (a tidal bore), which can reach 2 m in height. However, the longest river entirely in England is the Thames,
which is 215 mi in length. There are many lakes in England; the largest is Windermere, within the aptly named <color=#3366CC>Lake</color>
<color=#3366CC>District</color>.
Most of England's landscape consists of low hills and plains, with upland and mountainous terrain in the north and west
of the country. The northern uplands include the Pennines, a chain of uplands dividing east and west, the Lake District
mountains in Cumbria, and the Cheviot Hills, straddling the border between England and Scotland. The highest point in
England, at 978 m, is Scafell Pike in the Lake District. The Shropshire Hills are near <color=#3366CC>Wales</color> while <color=#3366CC>Dartmoor</color> and Exmoor
are two upland areas in the south-west of the country. The approximate dividing line between terrain types is often
indicated by the Tees–Exe line.
The Pennines, known as the "backbone of England", are the oldest range of mountains in the country, originating from
the end of the <color=#3366CC>Paleozoic Era</color> around 300 million years ago. The geological composition is predominantly sedimentary,
featuring significant deposits of <color=#3366CC>sandstone</color> and <color=#3366CC>limestone</color>, alongside substantial coal seams. There are <color=#3366CC>karst</color>
landscapes in calcite areas such as parts of <color=#3366CC>Yorkshire</color> and <color=#3366CC>Derbyshire</color>. The Pennine landscape is high <color=#3366CC>moorland</color> in
upland areas, indented by fertile valleys of the region's rivers. They contain two national parks, the Yorkshire Dales and
the Peak District. In the West Country, Dartmoor and Exmoor of the Southwest Peninsula include upland moorland
supported by granite.
The English Lowlands are in the central and southern regions of the country, consisting of green rolling hills, including
the Cotswold Hills, Chiltern Hills, North and South Downs; where they meet the sea they form white rock exposures
such as the cliffs of Dover. The English Lowlands also include flat plains such as Salisbury Plain, the Somerset Levels,
the South Coast Plain and <color=#3366CC>The Fens</color>.
Climate
England has a <color=#3366CC>temperate</color> maritime climate: it is mild with temperatures not much lower than 0 °C in winter and not
much higher than 32 °C in summer. The weather is frequently damp and changeable. The coldest months are January
and February, the latter particularly on the English coast, while July is normally the warmest. Months with mild to warm
weather are May, June, September and October. Rainfall is spread fairly evenly throughout the year.
Important influences on the climate of England are its proximity to the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic Ocean</color>, its northern <color=#3366CC>latitude</color> and the
warming of the sea by the <color=#3366CC>Gulf Stream</color>. Rainfall is higher in the west, and parts of the <color=#3366CC>Lake District</color> receive more rain
than anywhere else in the country. Since weather records began, the highest temperature recorded was 40.3 °C on 19
July 2022 at Coningsby, <color=#3366CC>Lincolnshire</color>, while the lowest was 26.1 °C on 10 January 1982 in Edgmond, Shropshire.
Nature and wildlife
The fauna of England is similar to that of other areas in the <color=#3366CC>British Isles</color> with a wide range of vertebrate and invertebrate
life in a diverse range of habitats. National nature reserves in England are designated by Natural England as key
places for <color=#3366CC>wildlife</color> and natural features in England. They were established to protect the most significant areas of habitat
and of geological formations. NNRs are managed on behalf of the nation, many by Natural England themselves, but
also by non-governmental organisations, including the members of The Wildlife Trusts partnership, the National Trust,
and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds. There are 221 NNRs in England covering 110000 ha. Often they
contain rare species or nationally important populations of plants and animals. . The Environment Agency is a
non-departmental public body, established in 1995 and sponsored by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural
Affairs with responsibilities relating to the protection and enhancement of the environment in England. The secretary of
state for environment, food and rural affairs is the minister responsible for environmental protection, agriculture,
fisheries and rural communities in England.
England has a temperate oceanic climate in most areas, lacking extremes of cold or heat, but does have a few small
areas of <color=#3366CC>subarctic</color> and warmer areas in the South West. Towards the <color=#3366CC>North of England</color> the climate becomes colder and
most of England's mountains and high hills are located here and have a major impact on the climate and thus the local
fauna of the areas. Deciduous woodlands are common across all of England and provide a great habitat for much of
England's wildlife, but these give way in northern and upland areas of England to <color=#3366CC>coniferous</color> forests (mainly plantations)
which also benefit certain forms of wildlife. Some species have adapted to the expanded urban environment,
particularly the <color=#3366CC>red fox</color>, which is the most successful urban mammal after the <color=#3366CC>brown rat</color>, and other animals such as the
<color=#3366CC>common wood pigeon</color>, both of which thrive in urban and suburban areas.
Major conurbations
The Greater London Built-up Area is by far the largest urban area in England and one of the busiest cities in the world.
It is considered a <color=#3366CC>global city</color> and has a population larger than any other country in the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color> besides England
itself. Other urban areas of considerable size and influence tend to be in <color=#3366CC>northern England</color> or the <color=#3366CC>English Midlands</color>.
There are 50 settlements which have designated city status in England, while the wider <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color> has 66.

While many cities in England are quite large, such as <color=#3366CC>Birmingham</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sheffield</color>, <color=#3366CC>Manchester</color>, <color=#3366CC>Liverpool</color>, Leeds, <color=#3366CC>Newcastle</color>,
Bradford, <color=#3366CC>Nottingham</color>, population size is not a prerequisite for city status. Traditionally the status was given to towns
with diocesan cathedrals, so there are smaller cities like Wells, Ely, Ripon, Truro and Chichester.
Economy
England's economy is one of the largest and most dynamic in the world, with a <color=#3366CC>GDP per capita</color> of £37,852 in 2022. HM
Treasury, led by the chancellor of the exchequer, is responsible for developing and executing the government's <color=#3366CC>public</color>
<color=#3366CC>finance</color> policy and <color=#3366CC>economic policy</color>. Usually regarded as a mixed market economy, it has adopted many <color=#3366CC>free market</color>
principles, yet maintains an advanced <color=#3366CC>social welfare</color> infrastructure.
The economy of England is the largest part of the <color=#3366CC>UK's economy</color>. England is a leader in the chemical and
pharmaceutical sectors and in key technical industries, particularly aerospace, the arms industry, and the software
industry. London, home to the <color=#3366CC>London Stock Exchange</color>, the United Kingdom's main <color=#3366CC>stock exchange</color> and the largest in
Europe, is England's financial centre, with 100 of Europe's 500 largest corporations being based there. As of 2025,
London is the largest financial centre in Europe and the second largest in the world.
London has been named as the fastest growing technology hub in Europe, with England having over 100 unique tech
companies with a value of $1 billion or more. The Bank of England, founded in 1694 as private banker to the
government of England and a <color=#3366CC>state-owned institution</color> since 1946, is the United Kingdom's <color=#3366CC>central bank</color>. The bank has a
monopoly on the issue of banknotes in England and Wales, although not in other parts of the UK. The government has
devolved responsibility to the bank's Monetary Policy Committee for managing the monetary policy of the country and
setting interest rates.
England is highly industrialised, but since the 1970s there has been a decline in traditional heavy and manufacturing
industries, and an increasing emphasis on a more service industry-oriented economy. Tourism has become a
significant industry, attracting millions of visitors to England each year. The export part of the economy is dominated by
<color=#3366CC>pharmaceuticals</color>, automotives, <color=#3366CC>crude oil</color> and petroleum from the English parts of North Sea oil along with Wytch Farm,
<color=#3366CC>aircraft engines</color> and alcoholic beverages. The creative industries accounted for 7 per cent GVA in 2005 and grew at an
average of 6 per cent per annum between 1997 and 2005.
Agriculture is intensive, highly mechanised and efficient by European standards, producing 60% of food needs with
only 2% of the labour force. Two-thirds of production is devoted to livestock, the remainder to arable crops. The main

crops that are grown are <color=#3366CC>wheat</color>, <color=#3366CC>barley</color>, <color=#3366CC>oats</color>, <color=#3366CC>potatoes</color>, and <color=#3366CC>sugar beets</color>. England retains a significant fishing industry.
Its fleets bring home a variety of fish, ranging from <color=#3366CC>sole</color> to <color=#3366CC>herring</color>. England is also rich in natural resources including

<color=#3366CC>coal</color>, <color=#3366CC>petroleum</color>, <color=#3366CC>natural gas</color>, <color=#3366CC>tin</color>, <color=#3366CC>limestone</color>, <color=#3366CC>iron ore</color>, <color=#3366CC>salt</color>, <color=#3366CC>clay</color>, <color=#3366CC>chalk</color>, <color=#3366CC>gypsum</color>, <color=#3366CC>lead</color>, and silica.
Science and technology
Prominent English figures from the field of science and mathematics include Sir <color=#3366CC>Isaac Newton</color>, <color=#3366CC>Charles Darwin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Robert</color>

<color=#3366CC>Hooke</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alan Turing</color>, <color=#3366CC>Stephen Hawking</color>, <color=#3366CC>Edward Jenner</color>, <color=#3366CC>Francis Crick</color>, <color=#3366CC>Joseph Lister</color>, <color=#3366CC>Joseph Priestley</color>, <color=#3366CC>Thomas Young</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Christopher Wren</color> and <color=#3366CC>Richard Dawkins</color>.
England was a leading centre of the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color> from the 17th century. As the birthplace of the <color=#3366CC>Industrial</color>
<color=#3366CC>Revolution</color>, England was home to many significant inventors during the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Famous
English engineers include <color=#3366CC>Isambard Kingdom Brunel</color>, best known for the creation of the Great Western Railway, a
series of famous <color=#3366CC>steamships</color>, and numerous important bridges, revolutionising public transport and modern-day
engineering. <color=#3366CC>Thomas Newcomen</color>'s steam engine helped spawn the Industrial Revolution.
The Father of Railways, <color=#3366CC>George Stephenson</color>, built the first public inter-city railway line in the world, the Liverpool and
Manchester Railway, which opened in 1830. With his role in the marketing and manufacturing of the steam engine, and
invention of modern coinage, <color=#3366CC>Matthew Boulton</color> (business partner of <color=#3366CC>James Watt</color>) is regarded as one of the most
influential entrepreneurs in history. The physician <color=#3366CC>Edward Jenner</color>'s <color=#3366CC>smallpox vaccine</color> is said to have "saved more lives
... than were lost in all the wars of mankind since the beginning of recorded history."
Inventions and discoveries of the English include the <color=#3366CC>jet engine</color>; the first industrial <color=#3366CC>spinning machine</color>; <color=#3366CC>the first computer</color>
and the first modern computer; the <color=#3366CC>World Wide Web</color> along with <color=#3366CC>HTML</color>; the first successful human <color=#3366CC>blood transfusion</color>; the

motorised <color=#3366CC>vacuum cleaner</color>; the <color=#3366CC>lawn mower</color>; the <color=#3366CC>seat belt</color>; the <color=#3366CC>hovercraft</color>; the <color=#3366CC>electric motor</color>; <color=#3366CC>steam engines</color>; and
theories such as the Darwinian theory of <color=#3366CC>evolution</color> and <color=#3366CC>atomic theory</color>. Newton developed the ideas of <color=#3366CC>universal</color>

<color=#3366CC>gravitation</color>, <color=#3366CC>Newtonian mechanics</color>, and <color=#3366CC>calculus</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Robert Hooke</color> his eponymously named <color=#3366CC>law of elasticity</color>. Other
inventions include the iron plate railway, the thermosiphon, tarmac, the <color=#3366CC>rubber band</color>, the mousetrap, "cat's eye" road
marker, joint development of the <color=#3366CC>light bulb</color>, steam <color=#3366CC>locomotives</color>, the modern <color=#3366CC>seed drill</color> and many modern techniques and
technologies used in precision engineering.
English innovators made crucial contributions to computing from the earliest concepts to the microchip era. <color=#3366CC>Charles</color>
<color=#3366CC>Babbage</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ada Lovelace</color> conceived the first programmable computer, while <color=#3366CC>George Boole</color> created the binary logic
underlying all digital systems, known as <color=#3366CC>boolean logic</color>. <color=#3366CC>Alan Turing</color> defined the foundations of computing and pioneered
artificial intelligence, while <color=#3366CC>Tommy Flowers</color> built <color=#3366CC>Colossus</color>, proving electronic computing feasible. Sir Frederic Williams,
Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill developed the Manchester Baby, while <color=#3366CC>Sir Maurice Wilkes</color> developed <color=#3366CC>EDSAC</color>
contributing to the first stored-program computers that established modern computer architecture. Geoffrey Dummer
conceptualised the integrated circuit.
The <color=#3366CC>Royal Society</color>, formally <color=#3366CC>The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge</color>, is a <color=#3366CC>learned society</color> and
the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color>'s national academy of sciences. Founded on 28 November 1660, it is the oldest national scientific
institution in the world. The Royal Institution of Great Britain was founded in 1799 by leading English scientists,
including <color=#3366CC>Henry Cavendish</color>. Some experts claim that the earliest concept of a <color=#3366CC>metric system</color> was invented by John
Wilkins in 1668.
Scientific research and development remains important in the universities of England, with many establishing science
parks to facilitate production and co-operation with industry. Cambridge is the most intensive research cluster for
science and technology in the world. In 2022, the UK produced 6.3 per cent of the world's scientific research papers
and had a 10.5 per cent share of scientific citations, the third highest in the world (after the United States and China).
Scientific journals produced in England include <color=#3366CC>Nature</color>, the <color=#3366CC>British Medical Journal</color> and <color=#3366CC>The Lancet</color>. The Department for
Science, Innovation and Technology, secretary of state for science, innovation and technology, and minister of state for
science, research and innovation has responsibility for science in England.
Transport
The Department for Transport is the government body responsible for overseeing transport in England. The department
is run by the secretary of state for transport.
England has a dense and modern transportation infrastructure. There are many motorways in England, and many other
trunk roads, such as the A1 Great North Road, which runs through eastern England from London to Newcastle (much
of this section is motorway) and onward to the Scottish border. The longest motorway in England is the M6, from Rugby
through the North West up to the Anglo-Scottish border, a distance of 232 mi. Other major routes include: the M1 from
London to Leeds, the M25 which encircles London, the M60 which encircles Manchester, the M4 from London to South
Wales, the M62 from Liverpool via Manchester to East Yorkshire, and the M5 from Birmingham to Bristol and the South
West.
Bus transport across the country is widespread; major companies include Arriva, FirstGroup, Go-Ahead Group, Mobico
Group, Rotala and Stagecoach Group. <color=#3366CC>Bus rapid transit</color> originated in England with the Runcorn Busway opening in
1971. The red <color=#3366CC>double-decker buses</color> in London have become a symbol of England. National Cycle Route offers cycling
routes nationally.
Rail transport in England is the oldest in the world: passenger railways originated in England in 1825. Much of Britain's
10000 mi of rail network lies in England, covering the country fairly extensively. There is rail access to France and
Belgium through the <color=#3366CC>Channel Tunnel</color> (completed in 1994) with <color=#3366CC>Eurostar</color> or LeShuttle services.
Great British Railways is a planned state-owned public body that will oversee rail transport in Great Britain from 2024.
The Office of Rail and Road is responsible for the economic and safety regulation of England's railways. Crossrail was
Europe's largest construction project with a £15 billion projected cost, opened in 2022. High Speed 2, a high-speed
north–south railway line, is under construction since 2019.
There is a <color=#3366CC>rapid transit</color> network in two English cities: the <color=#3366CC>London Underground</color>, and the Tyne and Wear Metro in
<color=#3366CC>Newcastle upon Tyne</color>, Gateshead and <color=#3366CC>Sunderland</color>. There are several extensive tram networks, such as the
Manchester Metrolink, Sheffield Supertram, West Midlands Metro, Nottingham Express Transit, and Tramlink in South
London. England also has extensive domestic and international aviation links. The largest airport is <color=#3366CC>Heathrow</color>, which is
the world's second busiest airport measured by number of international passengers.
By sea there is ferry transport, both local and international, including from Liverpool to Ireland and the Isle of Man, and
Hull to the Netherlands and Belgium. There are around 4400 mi of navigable waterways in England, half of which is
owned by the Canal & River Trust, however, water transport is very limited. The <color=#3366CC>River Thames</color> is the major waterway in
England, with imports and exports focused at the Port of Tilbury in the Thames Estuary, one of the United Kingdom's
three major ports.
Energy
Successive governments have outlined numerous commitments to reduce <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color> emissions. Notably, the UK is
one of the best sites in Europe for wind energy, and wind power production is its fastest growing supply. Wind power
contributed 26.8% of UK electricity generation in 2022. England is home to Hornsea 2, the largest offshore wind farm in
the world, situated in waters roughly 89 kilometres off the coast of Yorkshire.
The Climate Change Act 2008 was passed in Parliament with an overwhelming majority across political parties. It sets
out emission reduction targets that the UK must comply with legally. It represents the first global legally binding <color=#3366CC>climate</color>
<color=#3366CC>change mitigation</color> target set by a country. UK government energy policy aims to play a key role in limiting <color=#3366CC>greenhouse</color>
<color=#3366CC>gas emissions</color>, while meeting energy demand. Shifting availabilities of resources and development of technologies also
change the country's energy mix through changes in costs.
The current energy policy is the responsibility of the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and Secretary of
State for Energy Security and Net Zero. The Minister of State for Business, Energy and Clean Growth is responsible for
green finance, climate science and innovation, and low carbon generation. In 2024, the United Kingdom was ranked 5
out of 180 countries in the Environmental Performance Index. A law has been passed that <color=#3366CC>UK greenhouse gas</color>
<color=#3366CC>emissions</color> will be net zero by 2050.
Healthcare
The National Health Service (NHS), is the publicly funded healthcare system responsible for providing the majority of
healthcare in the country. The NHS began on 5 July 1948, putting into effect the provisions of the National Health
Service Act 1946. It was based on the findings of the Beveridge Report, prepared by the economist and social
reformer, <color=#3366CC>William Beveridge</color>. The NHS is largely funded by general taxation and National Insurance payments; it
provides most of its services free at the point of use, although there are charges for some people for eye tests, dental
care, prescriptions and aspects of personal care.
The government department responsible for the NHS is the Department of Health, under the secretary of state for
health. Most of the department's expenses are on the NHS – £98.6 billion was spent in 2008–2009. Regulatory bodies
such as the General Medical Council and the Nursing and Midwifery Council are organised on a UK-wide basis, as are
non-governmental bodies such as the Royal Colleges.
The average <color=#3366CC>life expectancy</color> is 77.5 years for males and 81.7 years for females, the highest of the four countries of the
United Kingdom. The south of England has a higher life expectancy than the north, but regional differences seem to be
slowly narrowing: between 1991–1993 and 2012–2014, life expectancy in the North East increased by 6.0 years and in
the North West by 5.8 years.
Demographics
Population
With over 56 million inhabitants, England is the most populous country of the United Kingdom, accounting for 84% of
the combined total. England taken as a unit and measured against international states would be the 26th largest
country by population in the world.
The <color=#3366CC>English people</color> are British people. There is an English diaspora in former parts of the British Empire; especially the

<color=#3366CC>United States</color>, <color=#3366CC>Canada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Australia</color>, <color=#3366CC>South Africa</color> and <color=#3366CC>New Zealand</color>. Since the late 1990s, many English people have
migrated to Spain. Due in particular to the economic prosperity of South East England, it has received many economic
migrants from the other parts of the United Kingdom. There has been significant Irish migration. The proportion of
ethnically European residents totals at 81.7%, including White British, Germans and Poles, down from 94.1% in 1991.
Other people from much further afield in the former British colonies have arrived since the 1950s: in particular, about
7% of people living in England have family origins in the Indian subcontinent, mostly India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
About 0.7% are Chinese, 0.6% are Arabs. 4.0% of the population are black, from Africa and the Caribbean, especially
former British colonies, and 2.9% identified as multiracial or mixed.
In 2007, 22% of primary school children in England were from <color=#3366CC>ethnic minority</color> families, and in 2011 that figure was
26.5%. About half of the population increase between 1991 and 2001 was due to immigration.
England contains one indigenous national minority, the Cornish people, recognised by the UK government under the
Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities in 2014.
Language
<color=#3366CC>English</color>, today widely spoken around the world, originated in what is now England, where it remains the principal
tongue. According to a 2011 census, it is spoken well or very well by 98% of the population
<color=#3366CC>English language learning and teaching</color> is an important <color=#3366CC>economic activity</color>. There is no <color=#3366CC>legislation</color> mandating an official
language for England, but English is the only language used for official business. Despite the country's relatively small
size, there are many distinct regional accents.
Cornish died out as a community language in the 18th century but is being revived, and is now protected under the
European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages. It is spoken by 0.1% of people in <color=#3366CC>Cornwall</color>, and is taught to
some degree in several primary and secondary schools.
<color=#3366CC>State schools</color> teach students a <color=#3366CC>second language</color> or <color=#3366CC>third language</color> from the ages of seven, most commonly French,
Spanish or German. It was reported in 2007 that around 800,000 school students spoke a foreign language at home,
the most common being <color=#3366CC>Punjabi</color> and <color=#3366CC>Urdu</color>. However, following the 2011 census data released by the Office for
National Statistics, figures now show that Polish is the main language spoken in England after English. In 2022, <color=#3366CC>British</color>
<color=#3366CC>Sign Language</color> became an official language of England when the British Sign Language Act 2022 came into effect.
Religion
In the 2021 census, 46.3% of the population of England specified their religion as <color=#3366CC>Christian</color>, 36.7% answered that they
had no religion, 6.7% specified that they were <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color>, while 4.3% of the population belongs to other religions and 6%
did not give an answer. Christianity is the most widely practised religion in England. The <color=#3366CC>established church</color> of England
is the <color=#3366CC>Church of England</color>, which left communion with <color=#3366CC>Rome</color> in the 1530s when <color=#3366CC>Henry VIII</color> was unable to annul his
marriage to <color=#3366CC>Catherine of Aragon</color>. The church regards itself as both Catholic and <color=#3366CC>Protestant</color>.
There are High Church and Low Church traditions, and some Anglicans regard themselves as Anglo-Catholics,
following the Tractarian movement. The monarch of the United Kingdom is the supreme governor of the Church of
England, which has around 26 million baptised members (of whom the vast majority are not regular churchgoers). In
2016, research at St. Mary's University in London reported that 19.8% of the population of England and Wales
identified as Anglican. The Church of England forms part of the Anglican Communion, with the <color=#3366CC>Archbishop of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Canterbury</color> acting as its symbolic worldwide head. Many cathedrals and parish churches are historic buildings of
significant architectural importance, such as <color=#3366CC>Westminster Abbey</color>, York Minster, Durham Cathedral, and Salisbury
Cathedral.
The second-largest Christian denomination is the <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color>. Since its reintroduction after the Catholic
Emancipation, the Church has organised ecclesiastically on an England and Wales basis where there are 4.5 million
members (most of whom are English). In 2016, 8.3% of the population of England and <color=#3366CC>Wales</color> identified as Catholic.

There has been one Pope from England to date, <color=#3366CC>Adrian IV</color>, while saints <color=#3366CC>Bede</color>, <color=#3366CC>Anselm</color>, and <color=#3366CC>John Henry Newman</color> are
regarded as Doctors of the Church.
A form of <color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color> known as Methodism is the third largest Christian practice; it grew out of Anglicanism through

<color=#3366CC>John Wesley</color>. It gained popularity in the mill towns of <color=#3366CC>Lancashire</color> and <color=#3366CC>Yorkshire</color>, and amongst tin miners in <color=#3366CC>Cornwall</color>.

There are other nonconformist minorities, such as <color=#3366CC>Baptists</color>, <color=#3366CC>Quakers</color>, <color=#3366CC>Congregationalists</color>, <color=#3366CC>Unitarians</color> and <color=#3366CC>The Salvation</color>
<color=#3366CC>Army</color>.
The patron saint of England is <color=#3366CC>Saint George</color>; his symbolic cross is included in the flag of England. There are many
other English and associated saints, including Cuthbert, Edmund, Alban, Wilfrid, Aidan, <color=#3366CC>Edward the Confessor</color>, John
Fisher, <color=#3366CC>Thomas More</color>, Petroc, Piran, Margaret Clitherow and <color=#3366CC>Thomas Becket</color>. There are non-Christian religions
practised. <color=#3366CC>Jews</color> have a history of a small minority on the island since 1070. They were expelled from England in 1290
following the Edict of Expulsion, and were allowed back in 1656.
Especially since the 1950s, religions from the <color=#3366CC>former British colonies</color> have grown in numbers, due to immigration. <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>
is the most common of these, now accounting for around 5% of the population in England. <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> are next in number, adding up to 2.8% combined, introduced from India and <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>.
A small minority of the population practise ancient <color=#3366CC>Pagan religions</color>. Neopaganism in the United Kingdom is primarily
represented by <color=#3366CC>Wicca</color> and Neopagan witchcraft, <color=#3366CC>Druidry</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Heathenry</color>. According to the 2011 census, there are
roughly 53,172 people who identify as Pagan in England, including 11,026 <color=#3366CC>Wiccans</color>. 24.7% of people in England
declared <color=#3366CC>no religion</color>, compared with 14.6% in 2001. <color=#3366CC>Norwich</color> had the highest such proportion at 42.5%, followed by
Brighton and Hove at 42.4%.
Education
The Department for Education is the government department responsible for issues affecting people in England up to
the age of 19, including education. State-funded schools are attended by about 93% of English schoolchildren.
Education is the responsibility of the secretary of state for education.
Children between the ages of 3 and 5 attend nursery or an Early Years Foundation Stage reception unit within a
primary school. Children between the ages of 5 and 11 attend primary school, and secondary school is attended by
those aged between 11 and 16. State-funded schools are obliged by law to teach the National Curriculum; basic areas
of learning include <color=#3366CC>English literature</color>, English language, <color=#3366CC>mathematics</color>, science, art & design, citizenship, history,
geography, religious education, design & technology, computing, ancient & modern languages, music, and physical
education. The <color=#3366CC>Programme for International Student Assessment</color> coordinated by the <color=#3366CC>OECD</color> currently ranks the overall
knowledge and skills of British 15-year-olds as 13th in the world in literacy, mathematics, and science with the average
British student scoring 503.7, well above the OECD average of 493.
Although most English secondary schools are comprehensive, there are selective intake grammar schools to which
entrance is subject to passing the eleven-plus exam. Around 7.2 per cent of English schoolchildren attend private
schools, which are funded by private sources. Standards in state schools are monitored by the Office for Standards in
Education, and in private schools by the Independent Schools Inspectorate.
After finishing compulsory education, students take GCSE examinations. Students may then opt to continue into further
education for two years. Further education colleges (particularly sixth form colleges) often form part of a secondary
school site. A-level examinations are sat by a large number of further education students, and often form the basis of
an application to university. Further education covers a wide curriculum of study and <color=#3366CC>apprenticeships</color>, including
T-levels, BTEC, NVQ and others. Tertiary colleges provide both academic and vocational courses.
Higher education
Higher education students normally attend university from age 18 onwards, where they study for an <color=#3366CC>academic degree</color>.
There are over 90 universities in England, all but one of which are public institutions. The Department for Business,
Innovation and Skills is the government department responsible for higher education in England. Students are generally
entitled to student loans to cover <color=#3366CC>tuition fees</color> and living costs. The first degree offered to undergraduates is the
<color=#3366CC>bachelor's degree</color>, which usually takes three years to complete. Students are then able to work towards a postgraduate
degree, which usually takes one year, or a doctorate, which takes three or more years.
England's universities include some of the highest-ranked universities in the world. As of 2024, four England-based

universities, the <color=#3366CC>University of Cambridge</color>, <color=#3366CC>University of Oxford</color>, <color=#3366CC>Imperial College London</color>, and <color=#3366CC>University College</color>
<color=#3366CC>London</color>, are ranked amongst the top ten in the 2024 QS World University Rankings. The University of Cambridge,
founded in 1209, and the University of Oxford, founded in 1096, are the two oldest universities in the English-speaking
world.
The <color=#3366CC>London School of Economics</color> has been described as the world's leading social science institution for both teaching
and research. The London Business School is considered one of the world's leading business schools and in 2010 its
MBA programme was ranked best in the world by the <color=#3366CC>Financial Times</color>. <color=#3366CC>Academic degrees</color> in England are usually split
into classes: first class, upper second class, lower second class, third, and unclassified. The King's School, Canterbury
and King's School, Rochester are the oldest schools in the English-speaking world. Many of England's most well-known
schools, such as Winchester College, <color=#3366CC>Eton</color>, St Paul's School, Harrow School and Rugby School are fee-paying
institutions.
Culture
Architecture
Many ancient standing stone monuments were erected during the prehistoric period; amongst the best known are
<color=#3366CC>Stonehenge</color>, Devil's Arrows, Rudston Monolith and Castlerigg. With the introduction of <color=#3366CC>Ancient Roman architecture</color>

there was a development of <color=#3366CC>basilicas</color>, baths, <color=#3366CC>amphitheaters</color>, triumphal arches, <color=#3366CC>villas</color>, Roman temples, <color=#3366CC>Roman roads</color>,
Roman forts, stockades and aqueducts. It was the Romans who founded the first cities and towns such as London,
Bath, York, Chester and St Albans. Perhaps the best-known example is <color=#3366CC>Hadrian's Wall</color> stretching right across northern
England. Another well-preserved example is the Roman Baths at Bath, Somerset.
Early medieval architecture's secular buildings were simple constructions mainly using timber with <color=#3366CC>thatch</color> for roofing.
Ecclesiastical architecture ranged from a synthesis of Hiberno–Saxon monasticism, to Early Christian <color=#3366CC>basilica</color> and
architecture characterised by pilaster-strips, blank arcading, baluster shafts and triangular headed openings. After the
Norman conquest in 1066 various castles were created; the best known include the <color=#3366CC>Tower of London</color>, Warwick Castle,
Durham Castle and <color=#3366CC>Windsor Castle</color>.
Throughout the Plantagenet era, an English Gothic architecture flourished, with prime examples including the medieval
cathedrals such as Canterbury Cathedral, <color=#3366CC>Westminster Abbey</color> and York Minster. Expanding on the Norman base there
was also <color=#3366CC>castles</color>, <color=#3366CC>palaces</color>, great houses, universities and parish churches. Medieval architecture was completed with
the 16th-century Tudor style; the four-centred arch, now known as the Tudor arch, was a defining feature as were
<color=#3366CC>wattle and daub</color> houses domestically. In the aftermath of the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> a form of architecture echoing classical
antiquity synthesised with Christianity appeared, the English Baroque style of architect <color=#3366CC>Christopher Wren</color> being
particularly championed.
<color=#3366CC>Georgian architecture</color> followed in a more refined style, evoking a simple Palladian form; the Royal Crescent at Bath is
one of the best examples of this. With the emergence of <color=#3366CC>romanticism</color> during Victorian period, a <color=#3366CC>Gothic Revival</color> was
launched. In addition to this, around the same time the Industrial Revolution paved the way for buildings such as The
Crystal Palace. Since the 1930s various <color=#3366CC>modernist</color> forms have appeared whose reception is often controversial, though
traditionalist resistance movements continue with support in influential places.
Gardens
Landscape gardening, as developed by Capability Brown, set an international trend for the <color=#3366CC>English landscape garden</color>.
Gardening, and visiting gardens, are regarded as typically English pursuits. The English garden presented an idealised
view of nature. At large country houses, the English garden usually included lakes, sweeps of gently rolling lawns set
against groves of trees, and recreations of classical temples, <color=#3366CC>Gothic</color> ruins, bridges, and other picturesque architecture,
designed to recreate an idyllic pastoral landscape.
By the end of the 18th century, the English garden was being imitated by the French landscape garden, and as far
away as Pavlovsk, Saint Petersburg, the gardens of the future Emperor Paul. It also had a major influence on the <color=#3366CC>public</color>
<color=#3366CC>parks</color> and gardens which appeared around the world in the 19th century. The English landscape garden was centred
on the English country house and manor houses.
English Heritage and the National Trust preserve great gardens and landscape parks throughout the country. The RHS
Chelsea Flower Show is held every year by the Royal Horticultural Society and is said to be the largest gardening show
in the world.
Folklore
English folklore developed over many centuries. Some of the characters and stories are present across England, but

most belong to specific regions. Common folkloric beings include <color=#3366CC>pixies</color>, <color=#3366CC>giants</color>, <color=#3366CC>elves</color>, <color=#3366CC>bogeymen</color>, <color=#3366CC>trolls</color>, <color=#3366CC>goblins</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>dwarves</color>. While many legends and folk-customs are thought to be ancient, such as the tales featuring Offa of Angel and
Wayland the Smith, others date from after the Norman invasion. The legends featuring <color=#3366CC>Robin Hood</color> and his Merry Men
of <color=#3366CC>Sherwood</color>, and their battles with the Sheriff of Nottingham, are amongst the best-known of these.
During the <color=#3366CC>High Middle Ages</color> tales originating from Brythonic traditions entered English folklore and developed into the
<color=#3366CC>Arthurian myth</color>. These were derived from Anglo-Norman, Welsh and French sources, featuring <color=#3366CC>King Arthur</color>, <color=#3366CC>Camelot</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Excalibur</color>, <color=#3366CC>Merlin</color> and the Knights of the Round Table such as <color=#3366CC>Lancelot</color>. These stories are most centrally brought
together within <color=#3366CC>Geoffrey of Monmouth</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Historia Regum Britanniae</color> (History of the Kings of Britain).
Some folk figures are based on semi or actual historical people whose story has been passed down centuries. On 5
November people celebrate Bonfire Night to commemorate the foiling of the <color=#3366CC>Gunpowder Plot</color> centred on <color=#3366CC>Guy Fawkes</color>.
There are various national and regional folk activities, participated in to this day, such as Morris dancing, Maypole
dancing, Rapper sword in the North East, Long Sword dance in Yorkshire, Mummers Plays, bottle-kicking in
Leicestershire, and cheese-rolling at Cooper's Hill. There is no official national costume, but a few are well established
such as the Pearly Kings and Queens associated with cockneys, the Royal Guard, the Morris costume and Beefeaters.
Cuisine
Since the <color=#3366CC>early modern period</color> the food of England has historically been characterised by its simplicity of approach and
a reliance on the high quality of natural produce. During the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color> and the Renaissance, English cuisine enjoyed
an excellent reputation, though a decline began during the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> with increasing urbanisation. The
cuisine of England has, however, recently undergone a revival, which has been recognised by food critics with some
good ratings in Restaurants best restaurant in the world charts.
Traditional examples of English food include the Sunday roast, featuring a <color=#3366CC>roasted joint</color> (usually beef, <color=#3366CC>lamb</color>, chicken or
pork) served with assorted vegetables, Yorkshire pudding and <color=#3366CC>gravy</color>. Other prominent meals include <color=#3366CC>fish and chips</color> and
the full English breakfast (generally consisting of <color=#3366CC>bacon</color>, <color=#3366CC>sausages</color>, grilled tomatoes, fried bread, black pudding, baked
beans, <color=#3366CC>mushrooms</color> and eggs). Various <color=#3366CC>meat pies</color> are consumed, such as steak and kidney pie, steak and ale pie,
<color=#3366CC>cottage pie</color>, pork pie (usually eaten cold) and the Cornish pasty.
Sausages are commonly eaten, either as bangers and mash or as toad in the hole. Lancashire hotpot is a well-known
stew originating in the northwest. Some of the more popular cheeses are <color=#3366CC>Cheddar</color>, Red Leicester, Wensleydale,
Double Gloucester and Blue Stilton. Many Anglo-Indian hybrid dishes, <color=#3366CC>curries</color>, have been created, such as <color=#3366CC>chicken</color>
<color=#3366CC>tikka masala</color> and balti. Traditional English dessert dishes include <color=#3366CC>apple pie</color> and other fruit pies; spotted dick – all
generally served with <color=#3366CC>custard</color>; and, more recently, sticky toffee pudding. Sweet pastries include <color=#3366CC>scones</color> served with jam
or cream, dried fruit loaves, Eccles cakes and mince pies as well as sweet or spiced biscuits.
Common non-alcoholic drinks include tea and coffee; frequently consumed alcoholic drinks include wine, <color=#3366CC>ciders</color> and
English beers, such as bitter, mild, <color=#3366CC>stout</color> and brown ale.
Visual arts
The earliest known examples are the prehistoric rock and <color=#3366CC>cave art</color> pieces, most prominent in <color=#3366CC>North Yorkshire</color>,
Northumberland and <color=#3366CC>Cumbria</color>, but also feature further south, for example at Creswell Crags. With the arrival of Roman
culture in the 1st century, various forms of art such as statues, busts, glasswork and mosaics were the norm. There are
numerous surviving artefacts, such as those at Lullingstone and Aldborough. During the Early Middle Ages the style
favoured sculpted crosses and ivories, manuscript painting, gold and enamel jewellery, demonstrating a love of
intricate, interwoven designs such as in the Staffordshire Hoard discovered in 2009. Some of these blended Gaelic and
Anglian styles, such as the Lindisfarne Gospels and Vespasian Psalter. Later <color=#3366CC>Gothic art</color> was popular at Winchester and
Canterbury, examples survive such as Benedictional of St. Æthelwold and Luttrell Psalter.
The Tudor era saw prominent artists as part of their court; portrait painting, which would remain an enduring part of
English art, was boosted by German <color=#3366CC>Hans Holbein</color>, and natives such as Nicholas Hilliard built on this. Under the
Stuarts, Continental artists were influential especially the Flemish, examples from the period include <color=#3366CC>Anthony van Dyck</color>,
Peter Lely, Godfrey Kneller and William Dobson. The 18th century saw the founding of the <color=#3366CC>Royal Academy</color>; a

<color=#3366CC>classicism</color> based on the <color=#3366CC>High Renaissance</color> prevailed, with <color=#3366CC>Thomas Gainsborough</color> and <color=#3366CC>Joshua Reynolds</color> becoming two
of England's most treasured artists.
In the 19th century, <color=#3366CC>John Constable</color> and <color=#3366CC>J. M. W. Turner</color> were major landscape artists. The Norwich School continued
the landscape tradition, while the <color=#3366CC>Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood</color>, led by artists such as <color=#3366CC>Holman Hunt</color>, <color=#3366CC>Dante Gabriel</color>
<color=#3366CC>Rossetti</color> and <color=#3366CC>John Everett Millais</color>, revived the <color=#3366CC>Early Renaissance</color> style with their vivid and detailed style. Prominent
amongst 20th-century artists was <color=#3366CC>Henry Moore</color>, regarded as the voice of British sculpture, and of British modernism in
general. The Royal Society of Arts is an organisation committed to the arts.
Literature, drama and philosophy
Early authors such as <color=#3366CC>Bede</color> and <color=#3366CC>Alcuin</color> wrote in Latin. The period of Old English literature provided the epic poem
<color=#3366CC>Beowulf</color> and the secular prose of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, along with Christian writings such as Judith, <color=#3366CC>Cædmon</color>'s
<color=#3366CC>Hymn</color> and hagiographies. Following the Norman conquest <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> continued amongst the educated classes, as well as
an Anglo-Norman literature.

Middle English literature emerged with <color=#3366CC>Geoffrey Chaucer</color>, author of <color=#3366CC>The Canterbury Tales</color>, along with <color=#3366CC>Gower</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Pearl</color>

<color=#3366CC>Poet</color> and <color=#3366CC>Langland</color>. <color=#3366CC>William of Ockham</color> and <color=#3366CC>Roger Bacon</color>, who were <color=#3366CC>Franciscans</color>, were major philosophers of the
Middle Ages. <color=#3366CC>Julian of Norwich</color>, who wrote Revelations of Divine Love, was a prominent Christian mystic. With the
English Renaissance literature in the <color=#3366CC>Early Modern English</color> style appeared. <color=#3366CC>William Shakespeare</color>, whose works include

<color=#3366CC>Hamlet</color>, <color=#3366CC>Romeo and Juliet</color>, <color=#3366CC>Macbeth</color>, and <color=#3366CC>A Midsummer Night's Dream</color>, remains one of the most championed authors in
<color=#3366CC>English literature</color>.

<color=#3366CC>Christopher Marlowe</color>, <color=#3366CC>Edmund Spenser</color>, <color=#3366CC>Philip Sydney</color>, Thomas Kyd, <color=#3366CC>John Donne</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Ben Jonson</color> are other

established authors of the Elizabethan age. <color=#3366CC>Francis Bacon</color> and <color=#3366CC>Thomas Hobbes</color> wrote on <color=#3366CC>empiricism</color> and <color=#3366CC>materialism</color>,
including <color=#3366CC>scientific method</color> and <color=#3366CC>social contract</color>. Filmer wrote on the Divine Right of Kings. <color=#3366CC>Marvell</color> was the best-known
poet of the Commonwealth, while <color=#3366CC>John Milton</color> authored <color=#3366CC>Paradise Lost</color> during the Restoration.
This royal throne of kings, this sceptred isle, this earth of majesty, this seat of Mars, this other Eden, demi-paradise; this
fortress, built by nature for herself. This blessed plot, this earth, this realm, this England.

Some of the most prominent philosophers of the <color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color> were <color=#3366CC>John Locke</color>, <color=#3366CC>Thomas Paine</color>, <color=#3366CC>Samuel Johnson</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Jeremy Bentham</color>. More radical elements were later countered by <color=#3366CC>Edmund Burke</color> who is regarded as the founder of
conservatism. The poet <color=#3366CC>Alexander Pope</color> with his satirical verse became well regarded. The English played a significant

role in <color=#3366CC>romanticism</color>: <color=#3366CC>Samuel Taylor Coleridge</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lord Byron</color>, <color=#3366CC>John Keats</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mary Shelley</color>, <color=#3366CC>Percy Bysshe Shelley</color>, <color=#3366CC>William</color>
<color=#3366CC>Blake</color> and <color=#3366CC>William Wordsworth</color> were major figures.
In response to the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>, agrarian writers sought a way between <color=#3366CC>liberty</color> and tradition; William Cobbett,
<color=#3366CC>G. K. Chesterton</color> and Hilaire Belloc were main exponents, while the founder of guild socialism, Arthur Penty, and
cooperative movement advocate G. D. H. Cole are somewhat related. Empiricism continued through <color=#3366CC>John Stuart Mill</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Bertrand Russell</color>, while <color=#3366CC>Bernard Williams</color> was involved in analytics. Authors from around the <color=#3366CC>Victorian era</color> include

<color=#3366CC>Charles Dickens</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Brontë sisters</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jane Austen</color>, <color=#3366CC>George Eliot</color>, <color=#3366CC>Rudyard Kipling</color>, <color=#3366CC>Thomas Hardy</color>, <color=#3366CC>H. G. Wells</color> and

<color=#3366CC>Lewis Carroll</color>. Since then England has continued to produce novelists such as <color=#3366CC>George Orwell</color>, <color=#3366CC>D. H. Lawrence</color>, <color=#3366CC>Virginia</color>

<color=#3366CC>Woolf</color>, <color=#3366CC>C. S. Lewis</color>, <color=#3366CC>Enid Blyton</color>, <color=#3366CC>Aldous Huxley</color>, <color=#3366CC>Agatha Christie</color>, <color=#3366CC>Terry Pratchett</color>, <color=#3366CC>J. R. R. Tolkien</color>, and <color=#3366CC>J. K. Rowling</color>.
Performing arts
The traditional folk music of England is centuries old and has contributed to several genres prominently; mostly <color=#3366CC>sea</color>
<color=#3366CC>shanties</color>, <color=#3366CC>jigs</color>, hornpipes and <color=#3366CC>dance music</color>. It has its own distinct variations and regional peculiarities. Ballads featuring
Robin Hood, printed by Wynkyn de Worde in the 16th century, are an important artefact, as are John Playford's The
Dancing Master and Robert Harley's Roxburghe Ballads collections. Some of the best-known songs are <color=#3366CC>Greensleeves</color>,
Pastime with Good Company, Maggie May and Spanish Ladies amongst others. Many <color=#3366CC>nursery rhymes</color> are of English
origin such as Mary, Mary, Quite Contrary, Roses Are Red, Jack and Jill, London Bridge Is Falling Down, The Grand
Old Duke of York, Hey Diddle Diddle and <color=#3366CC>Humpty Dumpty</color>. Traditional English Christmas carols include "<color=#3366CC>We Wish You</color>
<color=#3366CC>a Merry Christmas</color>", "The First Noel", "I Saw Three Ships" and "God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen".
Early English composers in classical music include Renaissance artists <color=#3366CC>Thomas Tallis</color> and <color=#3366CC>William Byrd</color>, followed by
<color=#3366CC>Henry Purcell</color> from the <color=#3366CC>Baroque period</color> and Thomas Arne who was well known for his patriotic song "<color=#3366CC>Rule, Britannia!</color>".
German-born <color=#3366CC>George Frideric Handel</color> spent most of his composing life in London and became a national icon in Britain,
creating some of the most well-known works of classical music, especially his English oratorios, <color=#3366CC>The Messiah</color>,
Solomon, <color=#3366CC>Water Music</color>, and Music for the Royal Fireworks.
Classical music attracted much attention in the 18th century with the formation of the Birmingham Triennial Music
Festival, which was the longest running classical music festival of its kind until the final concerts in 1912. The English
Musical Renaissance was a hypothetical development in the late 19th and early 20th century, when English
composers, often those lecturing or trained at the Royal College of Music, were said to have freed themselves from
foreign musical influences. There was a revival in the profile of composers from England in the 20th century led by

<color=#3366CC>Edward Elgar</color>, <color=#3366CC>Benjamin Britten</color>, Frederick Delius, <color=#3366CC>Gustav Holst</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ralph Vaughan Williams</color> and others. Present-day
composers from England include Michael Nyman, best known for <color=#3366CC>The Piano</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Andrew Lloyd Webber</color>, whose
musicals have achieved enormous success in the <color=#3366CC>West End</color> and worldwide.
In <color=#3366CC>popular music</color>, many English bands and solo artists have been cited as the most influential and best-selling

musicians of all time. Acts such as <color=#3366CC>the Beatles</color>, <color=#3366CC>Led Zeppelin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pink Floyd</color>, <color=#3366CC>Elton John</color>, <color=#3366CC>Queen</color>, <color=#3366CC>Rod Stewart</color>, <color=#3366CC>David</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bowie</color>, <color=#3366CC>the Rolling Stones</color> and <color=#3366CC>Def Leppard</color> are amongst the highest-selling recording artists in the world. Many musical
genres have origins in (or strong associations with) England, such as <color=#3366CC>British Invasion</color>, <color=#3366CC>progressive rock</color>, <color=#3366CC>hard rock</color>,

Mod, glam rock, <color=#3366CC>heavy metal</color>, <color=#3366CC>Britpop</color>, <color=#3366CC>indie rock</color>, <color=#3366CC>gothic rock</color>, shoegazing, acid house, garage, trip hop, <color=#3366CC>drum and bass</color>
and <color=#3366CC>dubstep</color>.
Large outdoor music festivals in the summer and autumn are popular, such as Glastonbury, V Festival, and the
Reading and Leeds Festivals. England was at the forefront of the illegal, free <color=#3366CC>rave</color> movement from the late 1980s,
which inspired the pan-European culture of teknivals. The Boishakhi Mela is a <color=#3366CC>Bengali New Year</color> festival celebrated by
the British Bangladeshi community. It is the largest open-air Asian festival in Europe. After the Notting Hill Carnival, it is
the second-largest street festival in the UK, attracting over 80,000 visitors.
The most prominent <color=#3366CC>opera house</color> in England is the <color=#3366CC>Royal Opera House</color> at Covent Garden. The Proms is a major
annual cultural event in the English calendar. The Royal Ballet is one of the world's foremost classical ballet
companies. The Royal Academy of Music is the oldest <color=#3366CC>conservatoire</color> in the UK, founded in 1822, receiving its <color=#3366CC>royal</color>
<color=#3366CC>charter</color> in 1830. England is home to numerous major orchestras such as the BBC Symphony Orchestra, the Royal
Philharmonic Orchestra, the Philharmonia Orchestra, and the London Symphony Orchestra. Other forms of
entertainment that originated in England include the <color=#3366CC>circus</color> and the <color=#3366CC>pantomime</color>.
Cinema
England has had a considerable influence on the history of the cinema, producing some of the greatest actors,

directors and motion pictures of all time, including <color=#3366CC>Alfred Hitchcock</color>, <color=#3366CC>Charlie Chaplin</color>, <color=#3366CC>David Lean</color>, <color=#3366CC>Laurence Olivier</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Vivien Leigh</color>, <color=#3366CC>John Gielgud</color>, <color=#3366CC>Peter Sellers</color>, <color=#3366CC>Julie Andrews</color>, <color=#3366CC>Michael Caine</color>, <color=#3366CC>Gary Oldman</color>, <color=#3366CC>Helen Mirren</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kate Winslet</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Daniel Day-Lewis</color>. Hitchcock and Lean are amongst the most critically acclaimed filmmakers. Hitchcock's The Lodger:
A Story of the London Fog (1926) helped shape the <color=#3366CC>thriller</color> genre in film, while his 1929 Blackmail is often regarded as
the first British sound feature film.
Major film studios in England include Pinewood, Elstree and Shepperton. Some of the most commercially successful
films of all time have been produced in England, including two of the highest-grossing film franchises (<color=#3366CC>Harry Potter</color> and
James Bond). Ealing Studios in London has a claim to being the oldest continuously working film studio in the world.
Famous for recording many motion picture <color=#3366CC>film scores</color>, the London Symphony Orchestra first performed film music in
1935. The Hammer Horror films starring <color=#3366CC>Christopher Lee</color> saw the production of the first gory horror films showing blood
and guts in colour.
The BFI Top 100 British films includes <color=#3366CC>Monty Python's Life of Brian</color> (1979), a film regularly voted the funniest of all time
by the UK public. English producers are also active in international co-productions and English actors, directors and
crew feature regularly in American films. The UK film council ranked David Yates, <color=#3366CC>Christopher Nolan</color>, Mike Newell,
<color=#3366CC>Ridley Scott</color> and Paul Greengrass the five most commercially successful English directors since 2001. Other
contemporary English directors include <color=#3366CC>Sam Mendes</color>, Guy Ritchie and Richard Curtis. Current actors include <color=#3366CC>Tom</color>

<color=#3366CC>Hardy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Daniel Craig</color>, <color=#3366CC>Benedict Cumberbatch</color>, Lena Headey, Felicity Jones, <color=#3366CC>Emilia Clarke</color>, Lashana Lynch, and <color=#3366CC>Emma</color>
<color=#3366CC>Watson</color>. Acclaimed for his motion capture work, Andy Serkis opened The Imaginarium Studios in London in 2011. The
visual effects company Framestore in London has produced some of the most critically acclaimed special effects in
modern film. Many successful Hollywood films have been based on English people, <color=#3366CC>stories</color> or events. The 'English
Cycle' of Disney animated films include Alice in Wonderland, The Jungle Book and Winnie the Pooh.
Sites and institutions
English Heritage is a governmental body with a broad remit of managing the historic sites, artefacts and environments
of England. It is currently sponsored by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. A non-governmental charity, the
National Trust holds a complementary role, focussed on landscapes and country houses. 17 of the 25 United Kingdom
UNESCO <color=#3366CC>World Heritage Sites</color> fall within England. Some of the best-known of these are: <color=#3366CC>Hadrian's Wall</color>, Stonehenge,
Avebury and Associated Sites, the <color=#3366CC>Tower of London</color>, the Jurassic Coast, Saltaire, Ironbridge Gorge, Blenheim Palace
and the <color=#3366CC>Lake District</color>.
London's <color=#3366CC>British Museum</color> holds more than seven million objects, one of the largest and most comprehensive collections
in the world, illustrating and documenting global human culture from its beginnings to the present. The <color=#3366CC>British Library</color> in
London is the national library and is one of the world's largest <color=#3366CC>research libraries</color>, holding over 150 million items in
almost all known languages and formats, including around 25 million books. The <color=#3366CC>National Gallery</color> in <color=#3366CC>Trafalgar Square</color>
houses a collection of over 2,300 paintings dating from the mid-13th century to 1900. The Tate galleries house the
national collections of British and international modern art; they also host the Turner Prize.
The secretary of state for culture, media and sport has overall responsibility for cultural property and heritage. A blue
plaque, the oldest historical marker scheme in the world, is a permanent sign installed in a public place in England to
commemorate a link between that location and a famous person or event. In 2011 there were around 1,600 museums
in England. Entry to most museums and galleries is free. <color=#3366CC>London</color> is one of the world's most visited cities, regularly
taking the top five most visited cities in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>. It is considered a global centre of finance, art and culture.
Media
The <color=#3366CC>British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC)</color>, founded in 1922, is the UK's publicly funded radio, television and Internet
